newsitem.title: USA: CME board to discuss halving S&P 500 contract.
newsitem.headline: CME board to discuss halving S&P 500 contract.

text.p: Directors will again discuss whether to split the size of the CME's Standard and Poor's 500 (S&P 500) contract at a special Chicago Mercantile Exchange board meeting Thursday afternoon.
The meeting is coming at a time when momentum appears to be growing for the exchange to halve the size of the S&P's multiplier in a bid to attract more trading interest, S&P 500 futures traders said.
"I think it's going to be a done deal," one S&P 500 futures trader said.
"It's a little more difficult to get size done in here; it's gotten pretty expensive to play this game and they've got to cut it."

The CME's benchmark equity product is currently worth $500 times the value of the index, and as S&P 500s have rallied, the value of the index has burgeoned. One contract this week was worth more than $475,000 and margin requirements to trade one S&P 500 contract have reached $17,500.
Some S&P 500 futures traders said they would welcome any plan to halve the contract, saying such a move would attract retail investors.

Others warned that cutting the contract's size would anger large institutional investors. Those investors could be unhappy trading twice as many contracts and paying double the commissions to hedge what one contract hedges now.
Some board members favored a smaller contract, saying the S&P 500 had become unwieldy for small and large investors alike.
"There's a lot of analysis going on and I'm sure we're going to come up with something creative," said Jack Bouroudjian, vice president of equity futures and options for Credit Agricole.
"I'm a big proponent of this," Bouroudjian said. "I think it's something we absolutely have to do."
In June, the CME announced it would debut a mini-S&P 500 futures contract.

"With this mini contract, I would think that could appease the retail customer," another S&P 500 futures trader said. "But there's obviously been a lot of press (about cutting the benchmark S&P 500) again," the trader said. "The bottom line is there is a faction here that is looking for any way to increase volume and increase participation."
Some traders noted that volume has stayed relatively flat, but others worried that halving the contract would dampen its overall success.

"You don't know what's going to happen because volume is going down, but it's only the summer," an S&P futures-options trader said. "Are you going to be Chicken Little and tell everybody the sky is falling when all it is is raining?"
"There are a lot of people who think cutting the contract in half is going to hurt them," he added. "The only one that's going to benefit is the exchange."
